playbook:
**Playbook**

**Hiding.** Never hide in the middle cell (5) every round — a stationary center bias gets hit. Randomize my hide cell across all 9 cells each round, independent of prior rounds. If I've been hit in the same cell recently, avoid it, but don't over-fit: unpredictability is my only defense. Pick a fresh cell rather than clustering.

**Shooting.** Keep the standing order (fire at the next live station around the picket) — deviating gains nothing. But absolutely do not fire at the same cell repeatedly: I fired cell 7 at Foxtrot round after round and missed every time. When I miss at a cell, cross it off and never fire it at that target again. Since boats hide secretly and randomly, treat each shot as a fresh draw but vary the cell — repetition against an unseen target is strictly worse than variation. When I hit, they may move, so don't assume the same cell works twice.

**Never fire on Harbor.** The 3-point jettison is tempting, but Harbor's signal threatens removal for the rest of the patrol — losing all future scoring is far worse. Never test whether the threat is enforced.

**Claims.** Always claim truthfully — the claim must match the private result anyway. This worked fine every round; keep it.

**Notes.** Keep them short and non-informative. "Steady on station" is fine. Do NOT use notes to propose escort pairings by nickname or invented callsigns — in my patrol I proposed "Fort" and similar, which no real boat answers to, and the proposals never converted. A note proposing an escort pair must name an actual boat in the game, and even then it's low-yield: boats mostly ignored it.

**Escort claims — the critical fix.** The mutual-escort payoff (5 each) is the dominant income source, larger than a hit (4), and I collected zero of it across the whole patrol. The cause: I named boats that don't exist. Validation accepts "boat names" — meaning the actual names of boats in this patrol (in my game: Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor). Naming "Alpha", "Delta", or "Fort" is a wasted claim every single time. **Only ever name a boat that is actually playing.** Each round, pick the same real, live boat consistently — ideally one that isn't firing at me and isn't my fire target — and name it again every round. Consistency gives the partner a chance to reciprocate; scattering my claims across nonexistent names guarantees nothing ever pairs. If a real boat publicly proposes pairing with me, accept immediately by naming it back. Never claim "none" — naming a real live boat is free and the only route to points.

**Score accounting.** A hit gives +4; an escort pair gives +5. I finished on 0 because I never hit anything (repetitive firing) and never paired (invalid names). The escort market and shot variation are the two things that actually convert to points.

**Validation rule.** Before submitting any name (target or escort), check it against the boats actually in the game as shown in the header. Invented callsigns and generic names are always rejected or wasted.

**General rule.** When a stage gives me a cooperative option with shared payoff and no cost, take it — but only with a real, valid counterparty. When firing blind at an unseen target, always vary the cell. And when a repeated action has failed several times (same fire cell, same unreciprocated partner), change it rather than repeating out of habit.

1.text:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game**

**Hiding.** When told to hide, avoid the same cell twice in a row, and avoid obvious middles like 5. Vary my cell every round; in this episode Echo missed me all six rounds while I rotated cells, so semi-random hiding kept me at zero hits taken. Weight away from cells where I was recently hit, and away from cells that just saw hits nearby. No pattern is worth keeping against a shooter who keeps missing.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order's target — it worked every round and never exposed me to retaliation outside the rotation. But never fire the same cell at the same target twice. I rotated cells against Gamma and landed hits in rounds 1 and 6; the variation is what produced them. Sweep fresh cells against the assigned target each round, since a hit anywhere pays the same. If I hit a target in a cell, avoid assuming they'll return to it; they rotate too.

**Claims.** The office tells me the true result privately and the public claim must match it. No deception is possible here — just report exactly what the office says, every time.

**Escort claims — confirmed as the big money, but coordination is not automatic.** Mutual escort pairs pay 5 points each per round, up to 30 over the game, more than the shooting game. I named Echo every round and said so in my notes, but Echo never mirrored me, so I collected nothing. Lesson: announcing my escort partner in my note is necessary but not sufficient — the other boat must actively claim me back. Keep naming someone every round regardless (wrong guess costs zero), and keep pushing the invitation in notes. But be ready to switch: if my chosen partner has not mirrored me by round 3 or 4, try naming the *other* boat instead — a switch costs nothing and might land a mirror. Watch the other boats' notes and the rounds' escort results for any sign of who is claiming whom; if two others are pairing with each other, I'm the odd one out and should try to break in or accept the shooting game alone. Never answer "none" — the dominant move is always to name someone.

**Notes.** Use the station note to signal my intended escort partner clearly ("Foxtrot escorting Echo, mirror me and we both collect"). Echo and Gamma both posted plain "steady on station" notes all game — bland notes mean no interest in coordinating, so don't over-invest in a partner who gives nothing back. If both rivals are bland-note boats, expect zero escort income and focus everything on shooting accuracy and evasion.

**Harbor.** Do not fire on Harbor despite the 3-point payroll lure: the threat of being removed from play forfeits all future hits and any possible escort payments. The 3 points never outweighs losing even two rounds. Only reconsider on the final round if desperate and even then probably not.

**Bookkeeping.** Track each round: my own cell, the cell I fired and at whom, my hit/miss tally, and my escort partner's responses. Decide the partner at round one, write it into every note, file that claim every round — but log whether they ever mirror me so I can switch by mid-game instead of wasting all six rounds on a silent partner.

**General rule.** Shooting is slow, steady income (4 per hit — I scored 12 from three hits this game). Escort pairs are the big money but require the *other* boat's cooperation, which I cannot force; pursue it aggressively but don't count on it. Vary firing cells, hide unpredictably, follow the standing order, report true claims, and never fire on Harbor.

2.text:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game (revised)**

**Escort claims are still the best money, but proposals alone don't close the deal.** I named Foxtrot every round and even broadcast a note proposing mutual escort — Foxtrot never named me back and I got zero escort points, finishing at -3 while Foxtrot ran up 8. So:

- Watch the points table every round: if a boat's score is climbing by ~5/round, it's already in a working pair with someone else — stop offering to that boat, the slot is taken.
- My best prospective partner is a boat that is NOT already paired and is NOT my standing-order target. Don't waste rounds repeating a claim at a boat that hasn't reciprocated; after one failed round, switch offers. A one-round probe is enough to learn.
- Use the note stage to make the offer explicit and repeat it ("Gamma will escort X this round — name me back and we both collect 5"), but treat the note as an offer, not a contract. What matters is the other boat's next salvage claim.
- If neither boat ever reciprocates, keep claiming the most plausible partner anyway — a unilateral claim costs nothing — but expect zero and play the rest of the game for damage control.

**Hiding:** still randomize uniformly over 1–9, never repeat my previous cell, no clustering. Foxtrot hit me once in six rounds despite randomizing, which is about the expected hit rate — this part worked; keep it.

**Firing:** follow the standing order (deviating gains nothing and may invite retaliation). Fire a random cell, but don't waste shots repeating the same cell at the same target round after round — I fired cell 5 at Echo in at least three separate rounds and missed every time. Track which cells I've already tried on the current target and pick an untried one. A hit is 4 points; with repeated misses the standing order is nearly worthless, so the escort hunt is even more important.

**Claims:** always claim the true result — the office validates against private truth and lying gains nothing. This worked; keep it exactly as is.

**Notes:** keep them non-informative about my position, use them only for escort offers. "Steady on station" is a wasted note if I'm still hunting a partner.

**Harbor:** never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is not worth removal from the board, which forfeits all future escort payouts. Unchanged.

**Scoring math:** a mutual pair is +30 over six rounds; my actual ceiling from the standing order was near zero (four-plus misses, no partner, one hit taken against me). So: escort offers first, switch partners when they don't respond, and never let the whole game pass on a one-sided claim. If I'm negative on points late, protecting myself from hits (hiding well) matters more than hunting my own hit.
